prayer.text: O Sacrament most holy, O Sacrament divine, all praise and all thanksgiving be every moment thine.

cues.text: On the morning of October 12, 2008, at St. Anthony of Padua Church in Sokolka, Poland, Father Filip Zdrodowski was celebrating Mass with Father Jacek Ingielewicz assisting in the distribution of Communion.
During the distribution, a consecrated Host slipped accidentally from the priest's hands onto the altar step; a kneeling parishioner noticed and pointed it out.
Placed in Water, as Custom Directs

Following standard Church procedure for a fallen Host, Father Jacek placed it in the vasculum, the small vessel of water priests use to rinse their fingers after distributing Communion, intending it to dissolve naturally.
The vessel was later transferred, for safekeeping, into the sacristy safe.
A week later, on October 19, the sacristan opened the safe to check on the Host.
He found it still visibly intact rather than dissolved, with a curved, bright red stain resembling blood at its center; the surrounding water showed no discoloration at all.
The parish reported the matter to Archbishop Edward Ozorowski of Bialystok, who ordered the Host preserved and had it transferred to the tabernacle of the rectory's Divine Mercy Chapel.

On January 7, 2009, samples of the stained tissue were examined independently, at the Medical University of Bialystok, by two specialists in pathological anatomy, Professor Maria Sobaniec-Lotowska and Professor Stanislaw Sulkowski.
Their joint declaration described the sample as most closely resembling myocardial tissue — heart muscle — among all living tissues they might have compared it to.
Both scientists stated that no natural or artificial process could account for what they had examined.
The Metropolitan Curia of Bialystok formally documented and confirmed the sequence of events.

The relic remains preserved at St. Anthony of Padua Church in Sokolka, one of the small number of twenty-first-century Eucharistic accounts to have undergone rigorous, named, independently conducted forensic examination.
Alongside the Buenos Aires and Tixtla cases from the same period, Sokolka is often cited by researchers as among the most thoroughly documented modern instances.
Some scholarly criticism has also been directed at aspects of how the initial investigation was conducted.
